entities.name: Zipoetes II of Bithynia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Zipoetes II, also known as Zipoites II or Ziboetes II, was a short-lived claimant to the throne of Bithynia, a Hellenistic kingdom in northwestern Anatolia, reigning from 279 BCE until his death in 275 BCE. His brief but disruptive rule represents a critical moment in the early consolidation of the Bithynian monarchy under the Zipoetid dynasty, directly challenging the legitimate succession of his nephew, Nicomedes I. His rebellion, though ultimately unsuccessful, underscored the internal instability inherent in Hellenistic power transitions and forced Nicomedes to secure his position through both military action and strategic alliances.

Following the death of his brother, Zipoetes I, in 279 BCE, Zipoetes II immediately contested the succession of Nicomedes I, Zipoetes I's son. This fratricidal struggle plunged Bithynia into a period of civil war, a common feature of the Hellenistic Successor Kingdoms as dynastic stability was often tenuous. Zipoetes II managed to hold a significant portion of Bithynian territory for several years, demonstrating considerable military prowess or at least the ability to garner sufficient support to resist Nicomedes' initial attempts to dislodge him. Historical accounts suggest his claim was based on a perceived right to rule, though the specifics are not fully preserved.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: While not a major figure of conquest, Zipoetes II's rebellion was a critical internal conflict that shaped the early Bithynian monarchy and indirectly influenced Nicomedes I's decision to invite the Galatians into Anatolia, profoundly altering the region's geopolitical landscape.
